title: Physics-Based versus Data-Driven Classification of Single-Photon Quantum Emitters from Sparse Autocorrelation Data
authors: Nhat Minh Nguyen, Md Shakhawath Hossain, Duc Anh Ngo, Chaohao Chen, Xiaoxue Xu, Toan Trong Tran, Carlo Bradac
abstract: Identifying single photon emitters from large, inhomogeneous candidate populations is key to realizing many quantum applications. This requires measuring the emitters second order autocorrelation function, whose statistical reliability is fundamentally limited by acquisition time. Machine learning classifiers can accelerate identification from sparse data, but their performance relative to physics-based inference has not been systematically examined. Here, we introduce sequential Bayesian inference for single photon emitter classification and benchmark it against Levenberg-Marquardt fitting and a feedforward neural network. We use synthetic training and test data calibrated against real Hanbury Brown-Twiss measurements from hexagonal boron nitride emitters, enabling evaluation against an exactly known ground-truth emitter number under realistic noise and background conditions. All three approaches achieve high, near-perfect accuracy with sufficient integration time, but differ greatly in convergence rate and robustness under sparse photon statistics. The neural network is most robust at short integration times. The Bayesian classifier reaches near-perfect accuracy fastest, while retaining full physical interpretability. Levenberg-Marquardt fitting remains a valuable, fully interpretable method, achieving the highest recall despite being the slowest to converge. These results lead to several key conclusions. No single method dominates across all performance metrics. Relying on any one metric alone can give a misleading picture of classifier performance, particularly under sparse photon statistics. Physics-based and data-driven methods are complementary rather than competing approaches. Together, these findings provide practical guidance for selecting and combining classification strategies for scalable single-photon-source screening and other quantum-emitter characterization tasks.
summary: This paper compares physics-based (Bayesian, LM) and data-driven (NN) machine learning techniques for identifying single-photon emitters from noisy, sparse autocorrelation measurements. By testing these methods on simulated data mimicking real Hanbury Brown-Twiss measurements, the authors conclude that these approaches are complementary, not competitive. The findings offer a roadmap for combining strategies to robustly characterize quantum sources.
main_problem: The core problem is reliably classifying single-photon quantum emitters (SPEs) from large, inhomogeneous populations using sparse second-order autocorrelation data.
main_result: No single classification method dominates; physics-based and data-driven approaches are complementary, with the Bayesian method offering the fastest convergence while retaining physical interpretability.
method: The study benchmarks three methods—Sequential Bayesian Inference, Levenberg-Marquardt fitting, and a Feedforward Neural Network—on synthetic data calibrated against real Hanbury Brown-Twiss measurements.
model_or_system: The system involves characterizing SPEs (e.g., in hBN) by measuring the second-order autocorrelation function, g^(2)(τ), which is sensitive to the emitter number N.
key_observables: The second-order autocorrelation function, g^(2)(τ), and its value at zero delay, g^(2)(0).
important_parameters: Integration time (determining data sparsity), background-to-signal ratio, and the number of emitters N.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on generating synthetic data via Monte Carlo simulations calibrated to real experimental noise and background conditions.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the experimental setup (HBT interferometer) and shows PL spectra and g^(2)(τ) measurements at various integration times. Other figures compare the performance curves of the different classification algorithms.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical challenge, details the three comparative classification methods (Bayesian, LM, NN), validates them using synthetic data derived from real measurements, and concludes by comparing their performance trade-offs regarding speed, robustness, and interpretability.
why_interesting: This work provides crucial practical guidance on how to combine advanced statistical inference (Bayesian) with machine learning (NN) for characterizing fundamental quantum sources, which is vital for scaling quantum technologies.
